## Confirmed arrangements

| Weight | 35% of the course grade |
| Duration | 120 minutes |
| Delivery | Individual paper examination; write directly in the booklet |
| Coverage | Cumulative course material, Weeks 1–15: MATLAB and R, with greater emphasis on R |
| Tasks | Eight questions and 28 subparts: eight one-mark conceptual MCQs and 20 written parts (code reading/repair, small calculations and evidence-based explanations) |
| Marks | 56 total: 14 MATLAB and 42 R; written parts carry 48 marks |
| References | Two A4 sheets, handwritten by you; both sides of each sheet may be used |

| Time | 09:00–11:00 UAE time |

The midterm's Weeks 1–6 cutoff and the quizzes' individual cutoffs do **not**
restrict the cumulative final. Approved individual accommodations follow the
usual university arrangements. This guide does not change the formal syllabus.

You are not expected to write long essays or a complete program from a blank
page. An answer might be a few values, a corrected expression, a calculation,
or a short explanation. Read the action requested in each part.

## Start here

1. Attempt the [separate practice paper](final-practice.qmd) individually, on
   paper, before consulting solutions. It is ungraded and needs no submission.
2. Mark each uncertainty as **syntax**, **calculation**, **interpretation** or
   **check**. Revisit the relevant strand below instead of rereading everything.
3. Redo the missed task without looking at the answer. Then change one input
   and predict what should change and what should stay the same.
4. Take unresolved questions and your attempted working to the TA or instructor.

The practice is not a question bank for the examination. Contexts, code,
numbers and combinations of ideas differ. Its revised eight-question,
56-mark format matches the planned final format, with eight one-mark MCQs
and 20 written parts. It samples the skills, not every topic that may be assessed.

## Revision map

Start with class examples, the companion explanations and selected **Core**
exercises. You do not need to complete every lab or optional extension.

| Strand | Be able to do this without running code | Where to revise |
|---|---|---|
| MATLAB foundations | Trace arrays, dimensions and indexing; distinguish matrix and element-wise operations; follow conditions and short loops; repair a function and design a revealing test | [Weeks 1–2](../weeks/week-01.qmd), [MATLAB recovery](../weeks/recovery-after-week-05.qmd) |
| Mathematical computation | Read polynomial coefficients; distinguish fitting, interpolation and extrapolation; calculate residuals/error; check roots, integrals and optima; preserve symbolic domains and compare admissible candidates | [Week 3](../weeks/week-03.qmd), [Week 4](../weeks/week-04.qmd), [Week 5](../weeks/week-05.qmd) |
| R foundations and exploration | Trace vectors and selections; keep paired observations aligned; explain missingness and denominators; interpret a labelled plot without a causal overclaim | [Weeks 6–8](../weeks/week-06.qmd), [companion index](../companion/index.html) |
| Data contracts | Explain types, missing-value encodings, row meaning and composite keys; reason about reshaping, factors, joins, unmatched rows and duplicated matches | [Week 9](../weeks/week-09.qmd), [Week 10](../weeks/week-10.qmd), [recovery](../weeks/recovery-after-week-10.qmd) |
| Reliable R programs | Use named checkpoints, function arguments, boundaries and edge-case tests; distinguish vectorization from iteration; retain every requested batch item, including failures; understand typed results | [Week 11](../weeks/week-11.qmd), [Week 12](../weeks/week-12.qmd), [recovery](../weeks/recovery-after-week-12.qmd) |
| Models and evidence | Interpret coefficients with units and conditioning; calculate predictions, residuals, MAE/RMSE; interpret R-squared against a same-row mean baseline; distinguish diagnostics, influence, sensitivity and new-data evaluation | [Week 13](../weeks/week-13.qmd), [Week 14](../weeks/week-14.qmd) |
| Communication and reproducibility | Read axes and reference lines; connect a caption to its observations; reconcile source, CSV, figure and report; identify a hidden workspace dependency and a clean-run check; qualify AI-written claims | [Week 15](../weeks/week-15.qmd), [Week 15 companion](../companion/week-15.html) |

For Weeks 13–14, understand what a coefficient interval or Cook's-distance flag
means and does not mean. Do not spend revision time deriving the Cook's-distance
formula or memorizing a full many-model program. Read supplied output and
explain the next justified check. Writing a Quarto report from scratch and
optional extension activities are not preparation requirements.

## Make an explanation specific

The useful habit is **answer + concrete check + interpretation + limitation**.
It is not an instruction to add four paragraphs to every part: supply what the
question actually requests.

| Incomplete answer | More useful answer |
|---|---|
| “Check the data.” | “Check that each requested group appears exactly once, including a status row for any failed fit.” |
| “The code runs, so it is correct.” | “The code runs; I still need a test whose expected value follows independently from the definition.” |
| “The residual is small, so that is the root.” | “Substitute the candidate into the original function and check that it belongs to the allowed domain; a small residual alone does not prove uniqueness.” |
| “The lowest RMSE wins.” | “Compare frozen predictions and a baseline on the same held-out rows. Training errors from different groups do not establish a common future-performance ranking.” |

For a numerical question, show substitutions and intermediate quantities.
For a code repair, respect the stated input/output contract, including missing
values, boundaries and supplied arguments. For a claim, name the population,
units, evidence and relevant limitation rather than writing only “not enough
information.”

## Using solutions and AI during revision

First make your own paper attempt. You may then use software, solutions or AI
to investigate a discrepancy, but read every line and check the result against
the mathematical definition or a separate small example. An AI explanation is
not an independent check merely because it sounds confident.

Close the aid and explain the reasoning again yourself. During the examination
there is no AI assistance or code execution. Your handwritten sheets should
contain distinctions, short examples you understand, and useful checks—not a
large program that you cannot trace.

## Marking and pacing

- Written tasks allow partial credit for correct method and reasoning;
  equivalent correct code and concise explanations are acceptable.
- A bare value may not earn all marks when working or justification is requested.
- For an MCQ, choose one answer. There is no negative marking.
- Exact fractions and square roots are acceptable unless otherwise specified.
- Scan the entire paper first. There are accessible marks throughout; move on
  when stuck and return later. Reserve time to check signs, units, IDs, domains
  and whether you answered every requested action.
